S is surjective. An element of (U + W)/W is (\u + \w) + W with \u \in U, \w \in W. Since (\u + \w) - \u = \w \in W, @lem-coset-equality (b) gives (\u + \w) + W = \u + W = S\u. \ker S = U \cap W. For \u \in U, S\u = W means \u \in W (@lem-coset-equality (b)), that is, \u \in U \cap W. By @thm-first-isomorphism applied to S, the rule \u + (U \cap W) \mapsto S\u = \u + W is a well-defined injective linear map with image \im S = (U + W)/W, hence an isomorphism. (Directly: if \u - \u' \in U \cap W, then \u - \u' \in W, so \u + W = \u' + W, and the value does not depend on the representative.) If U and W are finite-dimensional, then so is U + W (it is spanned by the union of bases, @prp-sum-of-spans), and @thm-dimension-quotient turns the theorem into \dim(U + W) - \dim W = \dim U - \dim(U \cap W). That is the dimension formula for sums (@thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim), now as a consequence of an isomorphism rather than of a basis computation. An exercise below asks for the details. The third theorem says that quotients can be taken in stages. [Third Isomorphism Theorem] Let U \subseteq W \subseteq V be subspaces. Then W/U = \{ \w + U : \w \in W \} is a subspace of V/U, and (V/U)/(W/U) 	o V/W, \qquad (\v + U) + W/U \mapsto \v + W is a well-defined isomorphism. Hence (V/U)/(W/U) \cong V/W. Let S \colon V/U 	o V/W, S(\v + U) = \v + W. Well defined. If \v + U = \v' + U, then \v - \v' \in U \subseteq W, so \v + W = \v' + W by @lem-coset-equality (b). By @thm-well-defined-on-quotient (a), applied to V 	o V/W, \v \mapsto \v + W, the rule defines a function on V/U. Linear and surjective. S((\v + U) + (\w + U)) = S((\v + \w) + U) = (\v + \w) + W = S(\v + U) + S(\w + U), and similarly for scalars, by @def-quotient-space in both quotients. Every \v + W equals S(\v + U). Kernel. S(\v + U) = W means \v \in W. If \v \in W, then \v + U \in W/U. Conversely, if \v + U = \w + U with \w \in W, then \v - \w \in U \subseteq W, so \v \in W. Hence \ker S = W/U. In particular W/U is a subspace of V/U, by @thm-prop-kernel. By @thm-first-isomorphism applied to S, (V/U)/(W/U) \cong \im S = V/W, via (\v + U) + W/U \mapsto S(\v + U) = \v + W. The notation W/U is used with two meanings, and they agree: the quotient space of W by U, and the set of cosets \w + U with \w \in W, sitting inside V/U. The coset \w + U is the same subset of V in both readings, and the operations agree because both are computed with representatives. For example, with V = 
R^3, U the z-axis and W the xz-plane, V/W \cong 
R through the y-coordinate, and the theorem says that first forgetting z and then forgetting x leaves the same thing as forgetting both at once. The universal property of the quotient The proofs of the three theorems repeated one move: a linear map that vanishes on U passes to V/U. We record that move once, in its general form. It is the standard way to define linear maps out of a quotient. [Universal Property of the Quotient] Let U be a subspace of V, \pi \colon V 	o V/U the quotient map, and T \colon V 	o W a linear map. 1. If U \subseteq \ker T, then there is exactly one linear map  ar T \colon V/U 	o W with  ar T \circ \pi = T, namely  ar T(\v + U) = T\v. Its image is \im T, and it is injective if and only if U = \ker T. 2. Conversely, if some function  ar T \colon V/U 	o W satisfies  ar T \circ \pi = T, then U \subseteq \ker T. (a) If \v - \v' \in U \subseteq \ker T, then T\v = T\v'. By @thm-well-defined-on-quotient (a) there is exactly one function  ar T with  ar T(\v + U) = T\v, and it is linear by the computation in the proof of @thm-first-isomorphism, which used only this formula. Any linear  ar T with  ar T \circ \pi = T satisfies this formula, so it is this one. The image is \{ T\v \} = \im T. The kernel of  ar T is \{ \v + U : \v \in \ker T \}; it is \{ U \}, the zero subspace, exactly when every \v \in \ker T lies in U, that is, when \ker T \subseteq U, which together with U \subseteq \ker T means U = \ker T. Apply @thm-injective-iff-trivial-kernel. (b) Let \u \in U. Then \pi(\u) = U = \pi(\0), so T\u =  ar T(\pi(\u)) =  ar T(\pi(\0)) = T(\0) = \0 by @thm-zero-maps-to-zero. Hence U \subseteq \ker T. In words: linear maps out of V/U are the same as linear maps out of V that kill U. The First Isomorphism Theorem is the case U = \ker T. For example, the map T \colon 
R^3 	o 
R, T(x, y, z) = x, kills the z-axis U, so it induces  ar T \colon 
R^3/U 	o 
R, (x, y, z) + U \mapsto x. Since \ker T is the yz-plane, strictly larger than U, this  ar T is not injective: it also kills the coset \e_2 + U. Quotients will return in Chapter 8, where an operator T with T(U) \subseteq U induces an operator on V/U, and this is the engine of induction arguments on the dimension. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the quotient space V/U and its two operations. 2. State the condition, in terms of \v - \w, for \v + U = \w + U. 3. True or false: V/U is a subspace of V. Justify your answer. 4. State the First Isomorphism Theorem. 5. If U is a 2-dimensional subspace of 
R^5, what is \dim(
R^5/U)? What is \dim(
R^5 	imes U)? 6. What must be checked before the formula (\v + U) + (\w + U) = (\v + \w) + U can be used as a definition, and which property of U makes the check work? (a) For a subspace U of V, V/U = \{ \v + U : \v \in V \}, with (\v + U) + (\w + U) = (\v + \w) + U and a(\v + U) = a\v + U (@def-quotient-space). (b) \v + U = \w + U if and only if \v - \w \in U (@lem-coset-equality). (c) False. The elements of V/U are cosets, which are subsets of V, not vectors of V. (d) If T \colon V 	o W is linear, then \v + \ker T \mapsto T\v is a well-defined isomorphism V/\ker T 	o \im T (@thm-first-isomorphism). (e) 5 - 2 = 3 by @thm-dimension-quotient, and 5 + 2 = 7 by @thm-dimension-of-product. (f) That the right-hand side does not depend on the representatives: if \v - \v' \in U and \w - \w' \in U, then (\v + \w) + U = (\v' + \w') + U. This works because (\v + \w) - (\v' + \w') = (\v - \v') + (\w - \w') and U is closed under addition. B. Practice [B1: A basis of a quotient of 
R^4] Let U = \Span((1, 0, 1, 0), (0, 1, 0, 1)) \subseteq 
R^4. 1. Find \dim(
R^4/U) and a basis of 
R^4/U. 2. Write (3, 1, 4, 1) + U in your basis. 3. Decide whether (1, 2, 3, 4) + U = (3, 4, 1, 2) + U. (a) The two spanning vectors are independent (look at the first two entries), so \dim U = 2 and \dim(
R^4/U) = 4 - 2 = 2 by @thm-dimension-quotient. Extend by \e_1, \e_2. If a(1, 0, 1, 0) + b(0, 1, 0, 1) + c\e_1 + d\e_2 = (a + c, b + d, a, b) = \0, then a = b = 0 from the last two entries and c = d = 0 from the first two. So the four vectors are independent, hence a basis of 
R^4 (@thm-right-size-basis), and by @thm-dimension-quotient (\e_1 + U, \e_2 + U) is a basis of 
R^4/U. (b) Solve (3, 1, 4, 1) = (a + c, b + d, a, b): a = 4, b = 1, c = -1, d = 0. Since the U-part becomes zero in the quotient, (3, 1, 4, 1) + U = -1(\e_1 + U) + 0(\e_2 + U). Check: (3, 1, 4, 1) + \e_1 = (4, 1, 4, 1) = 4(1, 0, 1, 0) + (0, 1, 0, 1) \in U. (c) The difference is (1, 2, 3, 4) - (3, 4, 1, 2) = (-2, -2, 2, 2). A vector (a, b, a, b) of U has equal first and third entries, but -2 
e 2. So the difference is not in U, and the cosets are different by @lem-coset-equality. [B2: A map that factors through a quotient] Let T \colon 
R[x]_{\le 2} 	o 
R^2, T(p) = (p(1), p'(1)), and U = \Span((x - 1)^2). 1. Show that U \subseteq \ker T, so that T induces a linear map  ar T \colon 
R[x]_{\le 2}/U 	o 
R^2 with  ar T(p + U) = T(p). 2. Prove that  ar T is an isomorphism. 3. Compute  ar T(x^2 + U), and find the coset  ar T^{-1}(0, 1). (a) T is linear, since evaluation and differentiation are. For q = (x - 1)^2, q(1) = 0 and q'(1) = 2(1 - 1) = 0, so T(q) = \0, and hence T(cq) = \0 for all c. So U \subseteq \ker T, and @thm-quotient-universal-property (a) gives the linear map  ar T. (b) T(1) = (1, 0) and T(x - 1) = (0, 1), so T is surjective and ank T = 2. By @thm-rank-nullity, \dim \ker T = 3 - 2 = 1 = \dim U, so \ker T = U by @thm-dim-impl-eq. By @thm-quotient-universal-property (a),  ar T is injective with image \im T = 
R^2. Hence  ar T is a linear bijection, an isomorphism. (c)  ar T(x^2 + U) = T(x^2) = (1, 2). Since T(x - 1) = (0, 1),  ar T^{-1}(0, 1) = (x - 1) + U, the set of all x - 1 + c(x - 1)^2. [B3: Matrices modulo scalars] Let n \ge 1 and S = \{ cI_n : c \in F \} \subseteq M_n(F). 1. Show that S is a subspace and find \dim(M_n(F)/S). 2. For n = 2, find a basis of M_2(F)/S. 3. Show that A + S = B + S if and only if A - B is a scalar matrix, and decide whether  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix} + S =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} + S. (a) S = \Span(I_n) is a subspace by @thm-span-subspace, of dimension 1 since I_n 
e 0. By @thm-dimension-quotient, \dim(M_n(F)/S) = n^2 - 1. (b) Extend (I_2) by E_{11}, E_{12}, E_{21}. If aI_2 + bE_{11} + cE_{12} + dE_{21} =  egin{pmatrix} a + b & c \ d & a \end{pmatrix} = 0, then a = c = d = 0 and then b = 0. So the four matrices are independent, hence a basis of M_2(F) (@thm-right-size-basis), and (E_{11} + S, E_{12} + S, E_{21} + S) is a basis of M_2(F)/S by @thm-dimension-quotient. (c) This is @lem-coset-equality (b) for the subspace S. Here the difference is  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = 2I_2 \in S, so the two cosets are equal. C. Going deeper [C1: The dimension formula from isomorphisms] Let U and W be finite-dimensional subspaces of a vector space V. 1. Using @thm-second-isomorphism and @thm-dimension-quotient, prove that \dim(U + W) = \dim U + \dim W - \dim(U \cap W). 2. Give a second proof: apply Rank–Nullity to the addition map S \colon U 	imes W 	o V, S(\u, \w) = \u + \w, after showing that \u \mapsto (\u, -\u) is an isomorphism from U \cap W onto \ker S. (a) U + W is finite-dimensional, being spanned by a basis of U followed by a basis of W (@prp-sum-of-spans), and U \cap W \subseteq U is finite-dimensional (@thm-subspace-dimension). By @thm-second-isomorphism, (U + W)/W \cong U/(U \cap W), and isomorphic finite-dimensional spaces have equal dimension (@thm-isomorphic-iff-same-dimension). Applying @thm-dimension-quotient to both sides, \dim(U + W) - \dim W = \dim U - \dim(U \cap W), which rearranges to the formula. (b) The map S is linear with image U + W by @thm-internal-external-direct-sum (a). Let J \colon U \cap W 	o U 	imes W, J\u = (\u, -\u); it is well defined because \u \in U and -\u \in W, and linear because the operations are entrywise. It is injective, since (\u, -\u) = (\0, \0) forces \u = \0. Its image lies in \ker S, since \u + (-\u) = \0. Conversely, if (\u, \w) \in \ker S, then \w = -\u; so \u = -\w \in W, hence \u \in U \cap W and (\u, \w) = J\u. Thus J is an isomorphism onto \ker S, and \dim \ker S = \dim(U \cap W). By @thm-dimension-of-product and @thm-rank-nullity, \dim U + \dim W = \dim(U 	imes W) = \dim(U + W) + \dim(U \cap W). [C2: The operator induced on a quotient] Let V be finite-dimensional, T \in \cL(V), and U a subspace with T\u \in U for every \u \in U. 1. Prove that  ar T(\v + U) \coloneqq T\v + U is a well-defined linear operator on V/U. 2. Let (\u_1, \dots, \u_m) be a basis of U, extended to a basis \sB = (\u_1, \dots, \u_m, \w_1, \dots, \w_s) of V. Show that [T]_{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} A & B \ 0 & D \end{pmatrix}, where A \in M_m(F) is the matrix of the restriction T|_U \colon U 	o U in (\u_1, \dots, \u_m), D \in M_s(F) is the matrix of  ar T in (\w_1 + U, \dots, \w_s + U), and 0 is the s 	imes m zero matrix. 3. Check (b) when T is differentiation on 
R[x]_{\le 2}, with U = 
R[x]_{\le 1} and \sB = (1, x, x^2). Hint: for (a), apply @thm-quotient-universal-property to \pi \circ T. (a) The map \pi \circ T \colon V 	o V/U, \v \mapsto T\v + U, is linear as a composition of linear maps (@thm-composition-linear). For \u \in U, T\u \in U, so (\pi \circ T)(\u) = U, the zero of V/U; thus U \subseteq \ker(\pi \circ T). By @thm-quotient-universal-property (a) there is exactly one linear map  ar T \colon V/U 	o V/U with  ar T(\v + U) = T\v + U. (b) For j \le m, T\u_j \in U, so it is a combination of \u_1, \dots, \u_m only, and its \sB-coordinates are 0 in the last s places. These first m columns, restricted to their first m entries, are the columns of the matrix A of T|_U (which maps U to U by hypothesis and is linear). For the remaining columns, write T\w_k = \sum_i b_{ik}\u_i + \sum_l d_{lk}\w_l. Passing to V/U, where \u_i + U = U is zero, gives  ar T(\w_k + U) = \sum_l d_{lk}(\w_l + U). So the s 	imes s matrix (d_{lk}) is the matrix D of  ar T in the basis (\w_1 + U, \dots, \w_s + U) of @thm-dimension-quotient, and the bottom-right block of [T]_{\sB} is D. (c) T(1) = 0, T(x) = 1, T(x^2) = 2x, so [T]_{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Differentiation maps U = 
R[x]_{\le 1} into itself. The block A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} is the matrix of T on U in (1, x), the lower-left block is  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, and the block D is the 1 	imes 1 matrix (0): indeed  ar T(x^2 + U) = 2x + U = U, the zero coset, since 2x \in U. [C3: Counting cosets over a finite field] Let F = 
F_q be a finite field with q elements, V a vector space over F of dimension n, and U a subspace of dimension m. 1. Show that \lvert V vert = q^n. 2. Show that every coset \v + U has exactly \lvert U vert elements, and deduce \lvert V/U vert = q^{n - m} by counting. 3. Check that (b) agrees with @thm-dimension-quotient. (a) Choose a basis (\v_1, \dots, \v_n). By @thm-unique-representation, (a_1, \dots, a_n) \mapsto a_1\v_1 + \dots + a_n\v_n is a bijection F^n 	o V, and F^n has q^n elements. (b) The map U 	o \v + U, \u \mapsto \v + \u, is surjective by @def-coset and injective because \v + \u = \v + \u' implies \u = \u'. So \lvert \v + U vert = \lvert U vert = q^m by (a) applied to U. By @lem-coset-equality (c), the cosets partition V into \lvert V/U vert disjoint sets of size q^m, so q^n = \lvert V/U vert \cdot q^m, and \lvert V/U vert = q^{n - m}. (c) By @thm-dimension-quotient, V/U is a vector space over 
F_q of dimension n - m, so by (a) it has q^{n - m} elements, in agreement with (b). For example, 
F_2^3 modulo a line has 8/2 = 4 cosets.

title: 3.10 Projections and the Trace of an Operator
content:
Projections and the Trace of an Operator Chapter 1 ended its discussion of complements with a promise: a splitting V = U \oplus W should give a projection of V onto U along W, and different complements should give different projections. This section keeps that promise. Projections are the operators that are simplest in a well-chosen basis, and computing their matrices there leads to a second topic: the trace of an operator, a number attached to T \in \cL(V) that no choice of basis can change. We end with involutions, which split a space into two pieces in the same way. Projections Suppose V = U \oplus W. By @def-direct-sum, every \v \in V can be written as \v = \u + \w with \u \in U and \w \in W in exactly one way. So the rule “\v \mapsto \u”, keep the U-piece and throw away the W-piece, is a well-defined function V 	o V. In 
R^3 = \{	ext{the } xy	ext{-plane}\} \oplus \{	ext{the } z	ext{-axis}\}, it sends (a, b, c) to (a, b, 0): the shadow of a point on the floor when light falls straight down. What property does such a map have that singles it out? Apply it twice. The output \u already lies in U, and its splitting is \u = \u + \0, so applying the rule again returns \u. Doing it twice is the same as doing it once. We take this as the definition, because it can be checked without knowing U and W in advance. A projection is an operator that leaves alone everything it has already produced. [Projection] Let V be a vector space over F. An operator P \in \cL(V) is a projection if P^2 = P, that is, P(P\v) = P\v for every \v \in V. In words: P^2 is the composite PP (@def-polynomial-of-operator), so the condition says that P fixes each of its own outputs. Equivalently, P\x = \x for every \x \in \im P: if \x = P\v, then P\x = P^2(\v) = P\v = \x, and conversely this for \x = P\v is P^2(\v) = P\v. No inner product and no notion of angle is involved. The projections of this section are often called oblique projections, to distinguish them from the orthogonal projections met later, in the chapters on inner product spaces. Examples. - Onto an axis. P(x, y) = (x, 0) on F^2. Then P^2(x, y) = P(x, 0) = (x, 0), so P^2 = P. - A rank-one projection. T(x, y) = (2x - y,\ 2x - y) on 
R^2 from @exm-projection-adapted-basis. We saw there that its matrix A satisfies A^2 = A; directly, T(2x - y, 2x - y) = (4x - 2y - 2x + y, \dots) = (2x - y, 2x - y). - Constant term. On F[x]_{\le n}, P(p) = p(0), the constant polynomial with value p(0). The constant polynomial c has value c at 0, so P(P(p)) = P(p). - Degenerate cases. The identity \id_V and the zero operator are projections, since \id_V^2 = \id_V and 0^2 = 0. They correspond to keeping everything and keeping nothing. Non-example by minimal change. Change the first example to T(x, y) = (2x, 0) on 
R^2. Its image is still the x-axis and its kernel is still the y-axis. But T^2(x, y) = (4x, 0) 
e T(x, y) when x 
e 0: T does not fix the vectors of its own image, since T(1, 0) = (2, 0). So having “the right image and kernel” is not enough; the clause P^2 = P is what forces P to be the identity on its image. Likewise the reflection R(x, y) = (y, x) is not a projection: R^2 = \id 
e R. Here is the promised correspondence. It says that projections and direct sum decompositions are two descriptions of the same thing. [Projections and Direct Sums] Let V be a vector space. 1. If P \in \cL(V) is a projection, then V = \im P \oplus \ker P, P is the identity on \im P, and P is zero on \ker P. 2. Conversely, suppose V = U \oplus W. Then there is exactly one operator P \in \cL(V) with P\u = \u for all \u \in U and P\w = \0 for all \w \in W, namely P(\u + \w) = \u. It is a projection, with \im P = U and \ker P = W. It is called the projection onto U along W. For (a), every vector splits as “what P keeps” plus “what P removes”: \v = P\v + (\v - P\v). The first piece is in the image by definition, and P^2 = P is exactly what puts the second piece in the kernel. For (b), uniqueness of the splitting makes the rule a function, and uniqueness again makes it linear. (a) Let \v \in V. Then \v = P\v + (\v - P\v), where P\v \in \im P and P(\v - P\v) = P\v - P^2(\v) = \0 because P^2 = P. Hence V = \im P + \ker P. If \x \in \im P \cap \ker P, then \x = P\x, as shown after @def-projection-operator, and P\x = \0; so \x = \0. By @thm-direct-sum-criteria, V = \im P \oplus \ker P. We have also seen that P fixes \im P, and P is zero on \ker P by definition. (b) Existence. By @def-direct-sum, each \v \in V has exactly one splitting \v = \u + \w, so P\v \coloneqq \u defines a function V 	o V. It is linear: if \v = \u + \w and \v' = \u' + \w', then \v + \v' = (\u + \u') + (\w + \w') and a\v = a\u + a\w are splittings, because U and W are subspaces, so by uniqueness P(\v + \v') = \u + \u' = P\v + P\v' and P(a\v) = a\u = aP\v. For \u \in U the splitting is \u = \u + \0, so P\u = \u; for \w \in W it is \w = \0 + \w, so P\w = \0. Properties. Every value P\v lies in U, and every \u \in U is P\u; so \im P = U. Then P(P\v) = P\v because P fixes U; so P^2 = P. Finally P(\u + \w) = \u is \0 exactly when \u = \0, that is, when \v = \w \in W; so \ker P = W. Uniqueness. If P' \in \cL(V) is identity on U and zero on W, then P'(\u + \w) = P'\u + P'\w = \u by linearity, so P' = P. So a projection is a direct sum decomposition V = U \oplus W, recorded as an operator: U is its image and W its kernel. Given P, the decomposition is \im P \oplus \ker P; given the decomposition, P is the projection onto U along W. The two constructions undo each other, by the “exactly one” in (b). Now the promise from Chapter 1. There, the x-axis U in 
R^2 had many complements, for instance the y-axis W and the line W' spanned by (1, 1). Each gives a projection onto the same line U. To project \v onto U along a complement, slide \v parallel to that complement until it hits U. Along the y-axis, (1, 2) = (1, 0) + (0, 2) gives P\v = (1, 0) (dashed arrow). Along W', (1, 2) = (-1, 0) + (2, 2) gives P'\v = (-1, 0) (dash-dotted arrow). In general P(x, y) = (x, 0) and P'(x, y) = (x - y, 0), with standard matrices  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. “Projection onto U” is incomplete: the direction “along W” matters. The two operators above are both projections, both have image U, and they are different: P(1, 2) = (1, 0) but P'(1, 2) = (-1, 0). Since U has infinitely many complements in 
R^2, it is the image of infinitely many projections. A projection is determined by its image and its kernel together. In finite dimension, the direct sum V = \im P \oplus \ker P hands us a basis in which P is as simple as possible. [The matrix of a projection] Let V be finite-dimensional and P \in \cL(V) a projection with ank P = r. Let (\u_1, \dots, \u_r) be a basis of \im P and (\w_1, \dots, \w_s) a basis of \ker P. Then \sB = (\u_1, \dots, \u_r, \w_1, \dots, \w_s) is a basis of V, and [P]_{\sB} =  egin{pmatrix} I_r & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \diag(1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots, 0), with r ones. By @thm-projection-direct-sum (a), V = \im P \oplus \ker P, so the concatenated list \sB is a basis of V by @thm-direct-sum-k-criteria ((a) ⇒ (d)). Since P\u_i = \u_i and P\w_j = \0, the columns of [P]_{\sB} are \e_1, \dots, \e_r followed by s zero columns (@def-matrix-of-linear-map). Conversely, an operator whose matrix in some basis is \diag(1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots, 0) is a projection, since that matrix squares to itself. With the change-of-basis square, this gives a way to write down any projection in standard coordinates. [Projecting onto a plane along a line] In 
R^3, let U = \{ (x, y, z) : x + y + z = 0 \} and L = \Span((1, 1, 1)), so that 
R^3 = U \oplus L by @exm-plane-line-direct-sum. Find the standard matrix of the projection P onto U along L, and check that it squares to itself. Direct route. By @exm-plane-line-direct-sum, (a, b, c) splits as  ig(a - m, b - m, c - m ig) + m(1, 1, 1) with m =  rac{a + b + c}{3}, and the first piece lies in U. So P(a, b, c) = \Big(	frac{2a - b - c}{3},\ 	frac{-a + 2b - c}{3},\ 	frac{-a - b + 2c}{3}\Big), \qquad [P]_{\sE} =  rac13 egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & -1 \ -1 & 2 & -1 \ -1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Adapted basis. (1, -1, 0) and (0, -1, 1) lie in U and are independent (look at the first and third entries), so they form a basis of the 2-dimensional plane U. With \sB = ((1, -1, 0), (0, -1, 1), (1, 1, 1)), @cor-projection-matrix gives [P]_{\sB} = \diag(1, 1, 0), and by @thm-change-of-basis-maps [P]_{\sE} = M\,\diag(1, 1, 0)\,M^{-1} with M = \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sE}, whose columns are the vectors of \sB. Multiplying out gives the same matrix as the direct route. Check. Let A be the matrix found. The first column of A^2 is A applied to  rac13(2, -1, -1), which is  rac19(4 + 1 + 1,\ -2 - 2 + 1,\ -2 + 1 - 2) =  rac13(2, -1, -1), the first column of A; the other columns work the same way by symmetry of the entries. Also A(1, 1, 1) = \0 and A(1, -1, 0) = (1, -1, 0), as a projection onto U along L must satisfy. The division by 3 needs 3 
e 0 in the field, which holds over 
R. Is P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} (acting on 
R^2) a projection? If so, onto which line, and along which line? P^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = P, so yes. Its image is spanned by its columns, \Span((1, 0)), the x-axis. Its kernel is \{ x + y = 0 \} = \Span((1, -1)). By @thm-projection-direct-sum, it is the projection onto the x-axis along the line y = -x. The trace of an operator For a projection of rank r, the diagonal matrix of @cor-projection-matrix has trace 1 + \dots + 1 = r \cdot 1. But traces are defined for matrices, and the same projection has many other matrices, such as the 3 	imes 3 matrix of @exm-projection-plane-along-line, whose trace is  rac{2 + 2 + 2}{3} = 2. The agreement is no accident. In @thm-trace-similarity-invariant we proved that similar matrices have the same trace, and by @thm-similar-iff-same-operator all matrices of one operator are similar. So the trace belongs to the operator. The trace of an operator is the trace of its matrix in any basis; the basis does not matter. [Trace of an operator] Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with \dim V \ge 1, and let T \in \cL(V). The trace of T is 	r T \coloneqq 	r [T]_{\sB}, where \sB is any basis of V. (For V = \{\0\} we set 	r T = 0.) In words: to find 	r T, choose a basis, write down the matrix of T with that same basis on input and output, and add the diagonal entries. Well-definedness. The definition names a basis but claims the answer does not depend on it. Let \sB and \sC be bases of V. By @thm-change-of-basis-maps, [T]_{\sC} = P^{-1}[T]_{\sB}P with P = \mtx{\id}{\sC}{\sB} invertible, so the two matrices are similar, and by @thm-trace-similarity-invariant they have the same trace. Hence 	r T depends only on T. Examples. - Identity. In every basis, [\id_V]_{\sB} = I_n, so 	r \id_V = n \cdot 1, where n = \dim V. Over 
R this is n; over 
F_2 it is 0 when n is even. - Differentiation. On F[x]_{\le n} with the basis (1, x, \dots, x^n), D(x^k) = kx^{k-1} has no x^k-component, so every diagonal entry of the matrix is 0 and 	r D = 0. - A shift of the variable. On 
R[x]_{\le 2}, let T(p) = p(x + 1). In (1, x, x^2), T(1) = 1, T(x) = 1 + x, T(x^2) = 1 + 2x + x^2, so the matrix is  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and 	r T = 3. - The reflection. R(x, y) = (y, x) has trace 0, whether computed from  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} or from \diag(1, -1) (@exm-reflection-diagonal-basis). The trace needs the same basis on both sides. For an operator T \in \cL(V), the matrix \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sC} with \sB 
e \sC is square, but its trace depends on the bases. For \id on 
R^2, with \sE the standard basis and \sC = ((2, 0), (0, 1)), we get \mtx{\id}{\sE}{\sC} = \diag(	frac12, 1), of trace 	frac32, while 	r \id = 2. Different bases on input and output give equivalent matrices, not similar ones, and equivalence does not preserve the trace. For the same reason there is no trace of a map V 	o W between different spaces. The rules for the trace of a matrix carry over at once. [Properties of the Trace of an Operator] Let V be finite-dimensional with n = \dim V, let S, T \in \cL(V) and c \in F. Then 	r(S + T) = 	r S + 	r T, \qquad 	r(cT) = c\,	r T, \qquad 	r(ST) = 	r(TS), \qquad 	r \id_V = n \cdot 1 . For n = 0 all traces are 0. Otherwise fix a basis \sB of V. The map T \mapsto [T]_{\sB} is linear by @thm-linear-maps-isomorphic-to-matrices, so [S + T]_{\sB} = [S]_{\sB} + [T]_{\sB} and [cT]_{\sB} = c[T]_{\sB}; and [ST]_{\sB} = [S]_{\sB}[T]_{\sB} by @thm-matrix-of-composition, and likewise for TS. The first three identities now follow from @thm-trace-properties, since 	r T may be computed in \sB. The last was computed in the examples. A first consequence: on a finite-dimensional space V of dimension n \ge 1 over a field in which n \cdot 1 
e 0, such as 
R, there are no operators with ST - TS = \id_V, since the left side has trace 0 and the right side has trace n \cdot 1. Now the trace of a projection. Over 
R it is simply the rank, but the precise statement is an equation in the field, and reading it as an equation of integers needs a hypothesis. [Trace of a Projection] Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F and P \in \cL(V) a projection. Then 	r P = (ank P) \cdot 1 \quad 	ext{in } F . If F has characteristic 0, or characteristic p > \dim V, then ank P is determined by 	r P: it is the unique integer r with 0 \le r \le \dim V and r \cdot 1 = 	r P. In particular ank P = 	r P for projections on real or complex spaces. Let r = ank P. If V = \{\0\}, both sides are 0. Otherwise, by @cor-projection-matrix there is a basis \sB with [P]_{\sB} = \diag(1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots, 0) with r ones, so 	r P = r \cdot 1 by @def-trace-operator. For the second statement, let n = \dim V. Since 0 \le r \le n and r \cdot 1 = 	r P, it remains to show uniqueness. Suppose k \cdot 1 = l \cdot 1 for integers 0 \le l \le k \le n. By @lem-integer-multiples, (k - l) \cdot 1 + l \cdot 1 = k \cdot 1 = l \cdot 1, and adding -(l \cdot 1) to both sides gives (k - l) \cdot 1 = 0. If k - l > 0, then by @def-characteristic the characteristic of F is non-zero and at most k - l \le n, which contradicts the hypothesis. Hence k = l. In 
R and 
C, r \cdot 1 is the number r. The hypothesis cannot be dropped. Over 
F_2, the identity of 
F_2^2 is a projection of rank 2, and its trace is 1 + 1 = 0, the same as the trace of the zero projection, of rank 0. The equation 	r P = (ank P) \cdot 1 still holds there; what fails is recovering the integer ank P from the field element 	r P. Involutions and reflections A projection satisfies P^2 = P. The other simple polynomial relation is T^2 = \id_V: doing T twice changes nothing. Such an operator is called an involution. Examples are the reflection R(x, y) = (y, x), the transpose A \mapsto A	p on M_n(F), and f(x) \mapsto f(-x) on functions 
R 	o 
R. In Chapter 1 the last two produced direct sums: symmetric plus skew-symmetric matrices (@exm-direct-sum-of-matrix), and even plus odd functions (@exm-even-odd-functions). The next theorem explains both at once. For an involution T, write E_{+} \coloneqq \{ \v \in V : T\v = \v \}, \qquad E_{-} \coloneqq \{ \v \in V : T\v = -\v \}. These are subspaces, since E_{+} = \ker(T - \id_V) and E_{-} = \ker(T + \id_V) (@thm-prop-kernel). [Involutions Split the Space] Let F be a field of characteristic not 2, V a vector space over F, and T \in \cL(V) with T^2 = \id_V. Then V = E_{+} \oplus E_{-}, and the projection onto E_{+} along E_{-} is  rac12(\id_V + T). Copy the even/odd split: \v =  rac12(\v + T\v) +  rac12(\v - T\v). Applying T swaps \v and T\v, so the first piece is fixed and the second changes sign. Both halves of the argument divide by 2, which is where the characteristic enters. Since the characteristic is not 2, 2 = 1 + 1 
e 0 in F (@def-characteristic), so  rac12 exists. Let \v \in V, and put \v_{+} =  rac12(\v + T\v) and \v_{-} =  rac12(\v - T\v). Then \v = \v_{+} + \v_{-}, and by linearity and T^2 = \id_V, T\v_{+} = 	frac12(T\v + \v) = \v_{+}, \qquad T\v_{-} = 	frac12(T\v - \v) = -\v_{-} . So \v_{+} \in E_{+}, \v_{-} \in E_{-}, and V = E_{+} + E_{-}. If \v \in E_{+} \cap E_{-}, then \v = T\v = -\v, so 2\v = \0 and \v =  rac12(2\v) = \0. By @thm-direct-sum-criteria, V = E_{+} \oplus E_{-}. The operator  rac12(\id_V + T) is linear by @thm-linear-maps-vector-space, sends \v to \v_{+}, fixes E_{+} (where T\v = \v) and kills E_{-} (where T\v = -\v). By the uniqueness in @thm-projection-direct-sum (b), it is the projection onto E_{+} along E_{-}. For the transpose, E_{+} is the symmetric and E_{-} the skew-symmetric matrices; for f(x) \mapsto f(-x), they are the even and odd functions; for the reflection R(x, y) = (y, x), they are the mirror line y = x and the perpendicular line y = -x, and the adapted basis ((1, 1), (1, -1)) is the one of @exm-reflection-diagonal-basis. In finite dimension, a basis of E_{+} followed by a basis of E_{-} gives [T]_{\sB} = \diag(1, \dots, 1, -1, \dots, -1), and so 	r T = (\dim E_{+}) \cdot 1 - (\dim E_{-}) \cdot 1. In Chapter 8 the non-zero vectors of E_{+} and E_{-} will be called eigenvectors with eigenvalues 1 and -1. In characteristic 2 an involution need not split the space. Over 
F_2, let T\x = J\x with J =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Then J^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I_2, since 2 = 0. But -1 = 1, so E_{-} = E_{+} = \ker(J - I_2) = \Span(\e_1), and E_{+} + E_{-} = \Span(\e_1) 
e 
F_2^2. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define a projection P \in \cL(V), and state the correspondence between projections and direct sum decompositions. 2. True or false: a projection is determined by its image. Justify your answer. 3. True or false: an operator T on 
R^2 with \im T the x-axis and \ker T the y-axis is a projection. Justify your answer. 4. Explain why 	r T does not depend on the basis used to compute it. 5. True or false: for every field F and every projection P on a finite-dimensional space over F, the integer ank P can be recovered from 	r P \in F. Justify your answer. 6. Where does the hypothesis “characteristic not 2” enter the proof of @thm-involution-decomposition? (a) P is a projection if P^2 = P (@def-projection-operator). By @thm-projection-direct-sum, a projection gives V = \im P \oplus \ker P, and each decomposition V = U \oplus W gives exactly one projection with image U and kernel W. (b) False. On 
R^2, P(x, y) = (x, 0) and P'(x, y) = (x - y, 0) are different projections with the same image, the x-axis. A projection is determined by its image and its kernel together. (c) False. T(x, y) = (2x, 0) has this image and kernel, but T^2 
e T. (d) Matrices of T in two bases are similar by @thm-change-of-basis-maps, and similar matrices have equal traces by @thm-trace-similarity-invariant. (e) False. Over 
F_2, \id on 
F_2^2 has rank 2 and the zero operator has rank 0, but both have trace 0. It is true when the characteristic is 0 or larger than \dim V (@thm-rank-equals-trace-projection). (f) Twice: to define \v_{\pm} =  rac12(\v \pm T\v), and to pass from 2\v = \0 to \v = \0. Both need 2 
e 0 in F. B. Practice [B1: A projection in 
R^3] Let U = \{ (x, y, z) \in 
R^3 : x + y - z = 0 \} and L = \Span((1, 1, 1)). 1. Show that 
R^3 = U \oplus L. 2. Find the standard matrix A of the projection P onto U along L. 3. Verify that A^2 = A, and that 	r A = ank A. (a) U is the kernel of (x, y, z) \mapsto x + y - z, which is non-zero; its image is then a non-zero subspace of 
R, hence all of 
R (@thm-dim-impl-eq), so \dim U = 3 - 1 = 2 by @thm-rank-nullity. If t(1, 1, 1) \in U, then t + t - t = t = 0, so U \cap L = \{\0\}. By @thm-direct-sum-criteria, \dim(U + L) = 2 + 1 = 3, so U + L = 
R^3 by @thm-dim-impl-eq, and 
R^3 = U \oplus L. (b) Split (a, b, c) = \u + t(1, 1, 1) with \u = (a - t, b - t, c - t) \in U: the condition (a - t) + (b - t) - (c - t) = 0 gives t = a + b - c. So P(a, b, c) = (-b + c,\ -a + c,\ -a - b + 2c), \qquad A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 1 \ -1 & 0 & 1 \ -1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Check: A(1, 1, 1) = \0, and for the vectors (1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 1) \in U, A(1, 0, 1) = (1, 0, 1) and A(0, 1, 1) = (0, 1, 1). (c) Row by row, A^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 0 + 1 - 1 & 0 + 0 - 1 & 0 - 1 + 2 \ 0 + 0 - 1 & 1 + 0 - 1 & -1 + 0 + 2 \ 0 + 1 - 2 & 1 + 0 - 2 & -1 - 1 + 4 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 1 \ -1 & 0 & 1 \ -1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = A . 	r A = 0 + 0 + 2 = 2, and ank A = ank P = \dim U = 2 by @thm-projection-direct-sum (b), in agreement with @thm-rank-equals-trace-projection. [B2: The complementary projection] Let P \in \cL(V) be a projection. 1. Prove that \id_V - P is a projection. 2. Prove that \im(\id_V - P) = \ker P and \ker(\id_V - P) = \im P. 3. Deduce that if P is the projection onto U along W, then \id_V - P is the projection onto W along U. (a) By @thm-composition-linear (composition distributes over sums of maps), (\id_V - P)^2 = \id_V - 2P + P^2 = \id_V - 2P + P = \id_V - P. (b) (\subseteq) P((\id_V - P)(\v)) = P\v - P^2(\v) = \0, so \im(\id_V - P) \subseteq \ker P. (\supseteq) If P\v = \0, then \v = (\id_V - P)(\v) \in \im(\id_V - P). For the kernel: (\id_V - P)(\v) = \0 means \v = P\v. Such \v lies in \im P, and conversely every \x \in \im P satisfies P\x = \x, as shown after @def-projection-operator. So \ker(\id_V - P) = \im P. (c) By @thm-projection-direct-sum (b), \im P = U and \ker P = W. By (a) and (b), \id_V - P is a projection with image W and kernel U. By the uniqueness in @thm-projection-direct-sum (b), applied to V = W \oplus U, it is the projection onto W along U. [B3: Traces of operators on matrices] 1. Let 	au \colon M_n(F) 	o M_n(F), 	au(A) = A	p. Show that 	r 	au = n \cdot 1. 2. Fix B \in M_2(F), and let L_B \colon M_2(F) 	o M_2(F), L_B(X) = BX. Show that 	r L_B = 2	r B. Hint: use the basis of matrix units E_{ij}. (a) Order the basis (E_{ij}) of M_n(F) in any way. Since 	au(E_{ij}) = E_{ji}, the coordinate column of 	au(E_{ij}) has a 1 in the position of E_{ji} and 0 elsewhere. The diagonal entry of the matrix in the column of E_{ij} is therefore 1 if E_{ji} = E_{ij}, that is i = j, and 0 otherwise. There are n basis vectors E_{ii}, so 	r 	au = n \cdot 1 by @def-trace-operator. (Consistently with @thm-involution-decomposition over 
R: symmetric matrices have dimension  rac{n(n+1)}{2}, skew-symmetric ones  rac{n(n-1)}{2}, and the difference is n.) (b) Use the basis (E_{11}, E_{12}, E_{21}, E_{22}) and write B = (b_{ij}). The product BE_{ij} has the i-th column of B in column j and zeros elsewhere, so BE_{ij} = b_{1i}E_{1j} + b_{2i}E_{2j}. The diagonal entry in the column of E_{ij} is the coefficient of E_{ij} itself, which is b_{ii}. Adding over the four basis vectors, 	r L_B = b_{11} + b_{11} + b_{22} + b_{22} = 2	r B. C. Going deeper [C1: When is a sum of projections a projection?] Let F have characteristic not 2, and let P, Q \in \cL(V) be projections. 1. Prove that P + Q is a projection if and only if PQ = QP = 0. 2. Show that (a) fails over 
F_2. 3. Suppose V is finite-dimensional over 
R and P + Q is a projection. Deduce that ank(P + Q) = ank P + ank Q. Hint: for (⇒) in (a), use the relation PQ + QP = 0 together with P^2 = P. (a) By @thm-composition-linear, (P + Q)^2 = P^2 + PQ + QP + Q^2 = P + Q + PQ + QP. (⇐) If PQ = QP = 0, this is P + Q. (⇒) If (P + Q)^2 = P + Q, then PQ + QP = 0. Multiplying on the left by P and using P^2 = P gives PQ + PQP = 0; multiplying on the right by P gives PQP + QP = 0. Subtracting, PQ - QP = 0, so PQ = QP. Then 2PQ = PQ + QP = 0, and since 2 
e 0 in F, PQ = 0. Hence also QP = 0. (b) Over 
F_2, let P = Q = \id_V with V 
e \{\0\}. Then P + Q = 2\id_V = 0, which is a projection, but PQ = \id_V 
e 0. The step from 2PQ = 0 to PQ = 0 is the one that fails. (c) By @thm-rank-equals-trace-projection over 
R, and @thm-trace-operator-properties, ank(P + Q) = 	r(P + Q) = 	r P + 	r Q = ank P + ank Q . [C2: The trace is the only trace-like functional] Let n \ge 1, and let \varphi \colon M_n(F) 	o F be linear with \varphi(AB) = \varphi(BA) for all A, B \in M_n(F). 1. Using E_{ij}E_{jk} = E_{ik} and E_{jk}E_{ij} = 0 for k 
e i, show that \varphi(E_{ik}) = 0 whenever i 
e k. 2. Show that \varphi(E_{ii}) = \varphi(E_{jj}) for all i, j. 3. Deduce that \varphi = c\,	r for some c \in F, and conversely that every c\,	r has the property. Recall that E_{ij}E_{kl} is E_{il} if j = k and 0 otherwise, by @def-matrix-multiplication. (a) Let i 
e k. Then E_{ik} = E_{ii}E_{ik} and E_{ik}E_{ii} = 0, because k 
e i. By the hypothesis and linearity, \varphi(E_{ik}) = \varphi(E_{ii}E_{ik}) = \varphi(E_{ik}E_{ii}) = \varphi(0) = 0. (b) E_{ii} = E_{ij}E_{ji} and E_{jj} = E_{ji}E_{ij}. Hence \varphi(E_{ii}) = \varphi(E_{ij}E_{ji}) = \varphi(E_{ji}E_{ij}) = \varphi(E_{jj}). (c) Let c = \varphi(E_{11}). For A = (a_{ij}) = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}E_{ij}, linearity with (a) and (b) gives \varphi(A) = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}\varphi(E_{ij}) = \sum_{i} a_{ii}\varphi(E_{ii}) = c\sum_i a_{ii} = c\,	r A . Conversely, c\,	r is linear and c\,	r(AB) = c\,	r(BA) by @thm-trace-properties. So the linear functionals with \varphi(AB) = \varphi(BA) are exactly the multiples of the trace.

title: Definition 0.1.1 (Negation, conjunction, disjunction)
content: Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be statements. The negation \(\neg P\) (“not \(P\) ”) is true when \(P\) is false, and false when \(P\) is true. The conjunction \(P \wedge Q\) (“ \(P\) and \(Q\) ”) is true when both \(P\) and \(Q\) are true, and false otherwise. The disjunction \(P \vee Q\) (“ \(P\) or \(Q\) ”) is true when at least one of \(P\) , \(Q\) is true, and false only when both are false.

title: Definition 0.1.2 (Implication, converse, contrapositive)
content: Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be statements. The implication \(P \Rightarrow Q\) (“if \(P\) then \(Q\) ”) is false when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false, and it is true in every other case. We call \(P\) the hypothesis and \(Q\) the conclusion . The converse of \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is the implication \(Q \Rightarrow P\) . The contrapositive of \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is the implication \(\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P\) .

title: Definition 0.1.4 (Negation of quantifiers)
content:
Let \(P(x)\) be a predicate with \(x\) ranging over \(S\) . Then \[ 
eg igl( orall x \in S : P(x) igr) \ \equiv\ \exists x \in S : 
eg P(x), \qquad 
eg igl(\exists x \in S : P(x) igr) \ \equiv\  orall x \in S : 
eg P(x). \] For a statement with several quantifiers, apply these rules from the outside in: each \( orall\) becomes \(\exists\) , each \(\exists\) becomes \( orall\) , the ranges stay the same, and the innermost condition is negated using @thm-de-morgan-logic .

title: Definition 0.1.3 (Quantifiers)
content: Let \(P(x)\) be a predicate whose variable \(x\) ranges over a fixed collection \(S\) . The universal statement \(\forall x \in S : P(x)\) (“for every \(x\) in \(S\) , \(P(x)\) ”) is true when \(P(x)\) is true for every element \(x\) of \(S\) , and false otherwise. The existential statement \(\exists x \in S : P(x)\) (“there exists \(x\) in \(S\) such that \(P(x)\) ”) is true when \(P(x)\) is true for at least one element \(x\) of \(S\) , and false otherwise. The symbols \(\forall\) and \(\exists\) are the universal and existential quantifiers .

title: Example (Negating simple quantified statements)
content:
Negate each statement, and say which of the statement and its negation is true. \( orall x \in 
R : x^2 \ge 0\) . \(\exists n \in 
Z : n 	ext{ is even and } n > 10\) . \( orall x \in 
R \ \exists y \in 
R : y > x\) .

title: Example (What “not injective” means)
content: A function \(f\) from \(A\) to \(B\) is called injective if \[ \forall a_1 \in A \ \forall a_2 \in A : \bigl( f(a_1) = f(a_2) \Rightarrow a_1 = a_2 \bigr). \] Write down, with no “not” in front, what it means for \(f\) to be not injective. Then show that \(f(x) = x^2\) , from \(\nR\) to \(\nR\) , is not injective.

title: Example (Negating “only the zero combination”)
content: Consider the pairs \((1, 2)\) , \((2, 4)\) , \((0, 1)\) , and the statement \[ \forall a, b, c \in \nR : \Bigl( a(1, 2) + b(2, 4) + c(0, 1) = (0, 0) \ \Rightarrow\ a = 0 \wedge b = 0 \wedge c = 0 \Bigr). \] Negate it, and decide which of the statement and its negation is true.

title: Example (What “not surjective” means)
content: A function \(f\) from \(A\) to \(B\) is called surjective if \[ \forall b \in B \ \exists a \in A : f(a) = b. \] Negate this, and show that \(f(x) = x^2\) , from \(\nR\) to \(\nR\) , is not surjective.

title: Exercise (C1: Exporting a hypothesis)
content: Prove that \(P \Rightarrow (Q \Rightarrow R)\) is logically equivalent to \((P \wedge Q) \Rightarrow R\) for all statements \(P, Q, R\) . Explain in one sentence why this lets a theorem with two hypotheses be stated either way.

title: Exercise (C2: When can a converse fail too?)
content: Determine whether there exist statements \(P\) and \(Q\) such that both \(P \Rightarrow Q\) and its converse \(Q \Rightarrow P\) are false. Justify your answer. Give predicates \(P(n)\) and \(Q(n)\) about integers such that both \(\forall n \in \nZ : \bigl(P(n) \Rightarrow Q(n)\bigr)\) and \(\forall n \in \nZ : \bigl(Q(n) \Rightarrow P(n)\bigr)\) are false. Explain why (a) and (b) do not contradict each other.

title: Theorem 0.1.1 (Contrapositive equivalence)
content: For all statements \(P\) and \(Q\) , the implication \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is logically equivalent to its contrapositive \(\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P\) .

title: Definition 0.2.2 (Divisibility and primes)
content: Let \(a\) and \(b\) be integers. We say \(a\) divides \(b\) , written \(a \mid b\) , if there exists an integer \(k\) with \(b = ak\) . An integer \(p\) is prime if \(p \ge 2\) and the only positive divisors of \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\) .

title: Definition 0.2.1 (Even and odd)
content: An integer \(n\) is even if there exists an integer \(k\) with \(n = 2k\) . An integer \(n\) is odd if there exists an integer \(k\) with \(n = 2k + 1\) .

title: Example (Refuting “every prime is odd”)
content: Decide whether every prime number is odd. Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: For each statement, name the proof technique you would use first (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, cases, induction, or counterexample), and give a one-sentence reason. Then carry out the proof or refutation. The sum of two odd integers is even. For every integer \(n\) , if \(3n + 2\) is odd, then \(n\) is odd. For every integer \(n \ge 1\) , \(3 \mid 4^n - 1\) . For every integer \(n \ge 1\) , \(n^2 \ge 2n\) . There is no largest integer.

title: Exercise (B1: Contrapositive)
content: Prove that for every integer \(n\) , if \(n^2\) is odd, then \(n\) is odd.

title: Exercise (B2: Induction)
content: Prove that for every integer \(n \ge 1\) , the sum of the first \(n\) odd numbers is \(n^2\) : \[ 1 + 3 + 5 + \cdots + (2n - 1) = n^2. \]

title: Exercise (B3: \sqrt{3} is irrational)
content: You may use the school fact that every integer has exactly one of the forms \(3k\) , \(3k + 1\) , \(3k + 2\) with \(k\) an integer. Prove that for every integer \(n\) , if \(3 \mid n^2\) then \(3 \mid n\) . Hence prove that there is no rational number whose square is \(3\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Stamps of 4 and 5)
content: Show that each of \(12, 13, 14, 15\) can be written as \(4a + 5b\) with \(a, b \in \nN\) . Prove by strong induction that every integer \(n \ge 12\) can be written as \(4a + 5b\) with \(a, b \in \nN\) . Show that \(11\) cannot be written in this form, so the bound \(12\) in (b) cannot be lowered to \(11\) . Hint: for \(n \ge 16\) , look at \(n - 4\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Division with remainder)
content: Let \(a\) and \(b\) be integers with \(b \ge 1\) . Let \(R\) be the collection of all non-negative integers of the form \(a - qb\) with \(q\) an integer. Show that \(R\) is non-empty. Let \(r\) be the least element of \(R\) , which exists by @thm-well-ordering , and write \(r = a - qb\) . Prove that \(0 \le r < b\) . Prove that the pair \((q, r)\) is unique: if \(a = qb + r = q'b + r'\) with \(0 \le r < b\) and \(0 \le r' < b\) , then \(q = q'\) and \(r = r'\) . Hint for (a): try \(q = -\lvert a \rvert\) .

title: Proposition 0.2.5 (Parity of a square)
content: For every integer \(n\) , \(n\) is even if and only if \(n^2\) is even.

title: Proposition 0.2.6 (Uniqueness of the identity)
content: Let \(\ast\) be a binary operation on \(S\) . Then \(\ast\) has at most one identity element.

title: Proposition 0.2.4 (n^2 + n is even)
content: For every integer \(n\) , the integer \(n^2 + n\) is even.

title: Proposition 0.2.9 (2^n > n)
content: For every natural number \(n\) , we have \(2^n > n\) .

title: Proposition 0.2.12 (Existence of a prime factor)
content: Every integer \(n \ge 2\) has a prime divisor.

title: Proposition 0.2.2 (Even squares)
content: For every integer \(n\) , if \(n^2\) is even, then \(n\) is even.

title: Proposition 0.2.8 (Sum of the first n integers)
content: For every integer \(n \ge 1\) , \[ 1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}. \]

title: Proposition 0.2.1 (Sum of even integers)
content: For all integers \(m\) and \(n\) , if \(m\) and \(n\) are even, then \(m + n\) is even.

title: Theorem 0.2.7 (Principle of Mathematical Induction)
content: Let \(n_0\) be an integer, and for each integer \(n \ge n_0\) let \(P(n)\) be a statement. Suppose ( base case ) \(P(n_0)\) is true, and ( inductive step ) for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) , if \(P(n)\) is true then \(P(n + 1)\) is true. Then \(P(n)\) is true for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) .

title: Theorem 0.2.13 (Infinitely many primes)
content: There are infinitely many prime numbers.

title: Theorem 0.2.3 (Irrationality of \sqrt{2})
content: There is no rational number whose square is \(2\) . That is, \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational.

title: Theorem 0.2.10 (Strong induction)
content: Let \(n_0\) be an integer, and for each integer \(n \ge n_0\) let \(P(n)\) be a statement. Suppose that for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) , \[ \text{if } P(k) \text{ is true for all integers } k \text{ with } n_0 \le k < n, \text{ then } P(n) \text{ is true.} \] Then \(P(n)\) is true for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) .

title: Theorem 0.2.11 (Well-Ordering Principle)
content: Every non-empty collection of natural numbers has a least element: an element \(m\) of the collection with \(m \le s\) for every \(s\) in the collection.

title: Definition 0.3.10 (Cartesian product)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. The Cartesian product of \(A\) and \(B\) is the set of ordered pairs \[ A \times B = \{ (a, b) : a \in A,\ b \in B \}. \] More generally, for sets \(A_1, \dots, A_n\) , the product \(A_1 \times \cdots \times A_n\) is the set of all ordered lists \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) with \(a_i \in A_i\) for each \(i\) .

title: Definition 0.3.1 (Common number sets)
content:
We write \(
N = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}\) for the natural numbers ; in this book \(
N\) includes \(0\) ; \(
Z = \{\dots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \dots\}\) for the integers ; \(
Q\) for the rational numbers , the numbers \(a/b\) with \(a, b \in 
Z\) and \(b 
e 0\) ; \(
R\) for the real numbers ; \(
C\) for the complex numbers , studied later in this chapter.

title: Definition 0.3.3 (Empty set)
content: The empty set \(\varnothing\) is the set with no elements: \(x \notin \varnothing\) for every object \(x\) .

title: Definition 0.3.9 (Unions and intersections of indexed families)
content: Let \(I\) be a set, and for each \(i \in I\) let \(A_i\) be a set. The collection \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) is an indexed family of sets, with index set \(I\) . Its union is \[ \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \{ x : \exists i \in I : x \in A_i \}, \] and, if \(I\) is non-empty , its intersection is \[ \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \{ x : \forall i \in I : x \in A_i \}. \]

title: Definition 0.3.7 (Intersection)
content: The intersection of sets \(A\) and \(B\) is \[ A \cap B = \{ x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B \}. \] We call \(A\) and \(B\) disjoint if \(A \cap B = \varnothing\) .

title: Definition 0.3.11 (n-tuples)
content: Let \(A\) be a set and \(n \ge 1\) an integer. An \(n\) -tuple of elements of \(A\) is an ordered list \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) with each \(a_i \in A\) . The set of all of them is \[ A^n = \underbrace{A \times A \times \cdots \times A}_{n \text{ factors}}. \] Two \(n\) -tuples are equal exactly when \(a_i = b_i\) for every \(i = 1, \dots, n\) .

title: Definition 0.3.12 (Power set)
content: The power set of a set \(S\) is the set of all subsets of \(S\) : \[ \powerset{S} = \{ X : X \subseteq S \}. \]

title: Definition 0.3.2 (Set-builder notation)
content: Let \(S\) be a set and let \(P(x)\) be a predicate for \(x \in S\) . The set \[ \{ x \in S : P(x) \} \] is the set whose elements are exactly those \(x \in S\) for which \(P(x)\) is true.

title: Definition 0.3.8 (Set difference and complement)
content: The difference of sets \(A\) and \(B\) is \[ A \setminus B = \{ x \in A : x \notin B \}. \] When all sets under discussion are subsets of one fixed set \(U\) , the complement of \(B \subseteq U\) is \(B^{c} = U \setminus B\) .

title: Definition 0.3.5 (Set equality)
content: Two sets \(A\) and \(B\) are equal , written \(A = B\) , if they have exactly the same elements: \[ \forall x : \bigl( x \in A \Leftrightarrow x \in B \bigr). \]

title: Definition 0.3.4 (Subset)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. We say \(A\) is a subset of \(B\) , and write \(A \subseteq B\) , if \[ \forall x : \bigl( x \in A \Rightarrow x \in B \bigr). \] If \(A \subseteq B\) and \(A \ne B\) , then \(A\) is a proper subset of \(B\) , written \(A \subsetneq B\) .

title: Definition 0.3.6 (Union)
content: The union of sets \(A\) and \(B\) is \[ A \cup B = \{ x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B \}. \]

title: Example (Indexed unions and intersections of intervals)
content: For each integer \(n \ge 1\) , let \(A_n = [1/n, 1]\) and \(B_n = (0, 1/n)\) . Show that \[ \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n = (0, 1] \qquad \text{and} \qquad \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} B_n = \varnothing. \] You may use the fact that for every real \(x > 0\) there is an integer \(n \ge 1\) with \(1/n < x\) .

title: Exercise (B1: The second De Morgan law)
content: Let \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) be sets. Prove that \(A \setminus (B \cap C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C)\) , which is part (b) of @thm-de-morgan-sets .

title: Exercise (B2: A distributive law)
content: Let \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) be sets. Prove that \(A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)\) , which is part (a) of @thm-distributive-sets .

title: Exercise (B3: An indexed intersection)
content: Prove that \[ \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} \Bigl( -\frac1n, \frac1n \Bigr) = \{0\}. \] You may use the fact that for every real \(x > 0\) there is an integer \(n \ge 1\) with \(1/n < x\) .

title: Exercise (C1: When union equals intersection)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Prove that \(A \cup B = A \cap B\) if and only if \(A = B\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Counting subsets)
content: For a finite set \(S\) , write \(\lvert S \rvert\) for its number of elements. The aim is to prove that \(\lvert \powerset{S} \rvert = 2^{\lvert S \rvert}\) for every finite set \(S\) . Check the claim when \(S = \varnothing\) . Let \(S\) have \(n + 1\) elements, fix \(s \in S\) , and let \(S' = S \setminus \{s\}\) . Show that every subset \(X\) of \(S\) belongs to exactly one of the two collections: the subsets of \(S\) with \(s \notin X\) , and the subsets of \(S\) with \(s \in X\) . Show that the subsets of \(S\) with \(s \notin X\) are exactly the subsets of \(S'\) , and that \(X \mapsto X \setminus \{s\}\) and \(T \mapsto T \cup \{s\}\) pair off the subsets of \(S\) containing \(s\) with the subsets of \(S'\) , each undoing the other. Hence prove the claim by induction on \(n = \lvert S \rvert\) . Hint: in (c), use double inclusion to check that \((X \setminus \{s\}) \cup \{s\} = X\) when \(s \in X\) .

title: Theorem 0.3.2 (De Morgan’s laws for sets)
content: Let \(A\) , \(B\) and \(C\) be sets. Then \(A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C)\) ; \(A \setminus (B \cap C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C)\) . In particular, if \(B, C \subseteq U\) , then \((B \cup C)^{c} = B^{c} \cap C^{c}\) and \((B \cap C)^{c} = B^{c} \cup C^{c}\) .

title: Theorem 0.3.3 (Distributive laws for sets)
content: Let \(A\) , \(B\) and \(C\) be sets. Then \(A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)\) ; \(A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)\) .

title: Theorem 0.3.1 (Double inclusion)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Then \(A = B\) if and only if \(A \subseteq B\) and \(B \subseteq A\) .

title: Definition 0.4.4 (Composition)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be functions. The composition \(g \circ f \colon X \to Z\) is defined by \[ (g \circ f)(x) \coloneqq g\big(f(x)\big) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X. \]

title: Definition 0.4.1 (Function)
content: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be sets. A function (or map ) \(f \colon X \to Y\) is a rule that assigns to every element \(x \in X\) exactly one element \(f(x) \in Y\) . The set \(X\) is the domain of \(f\) , the set \(Y\) is its codomain , and \(f(x)\) is the value of \(f\) at \(x\) . We also write \(x \mapsto f(x)\) . Two functions \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon X' \to Y'\) are equal if \(X = X'\) , \(Y = Y'\) , and \(f(x) = g(x)\) for every \(x \in X\) .

title: Definition 0.4.5 (Identity function)
content: For a set \(X\) , the identity function on \(X\) is \(\id_X \colon X \to X\) , \(\id_X(x) = x\) .

title: Definition 0.4.2 (Image and preimage)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function, \(A \subseteq X\) and \(B \subseteq Y\) . The image of \(A\) under \(f\) is \(f(A) \coloneqq \{ f(a) : a \in A \} \subseteq Y\) . The set \(f(X)\) is called the image of \(f\) . The preimage of \(B\) under \(f\) is \(f^{-1}(B) \coloneqq \{ x \in X : f(x) \in B \} \subseteq X\) .

title: Definition 0.4.3 (Injective, surjective, bijective)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. \(f\) is injective (one-to-one) if for all \(x_1, x_2 \in X\) , \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\) implies \(x_1 = x_2\) . \(f\) is surjective (onto) if for every \(y \in Y\) there exists \(x \in X\) with \(f(x) = y\) . Equivalently, \(f(X) = Y\) . \(f\) is bijective if it is both injective and surjective.

title: Definition 0.4.7 (Inverse function)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) . A function \(g \colon Y \to X\) is an inverse of \(f\) if \[ g \circ f = \id_X \qquad \text{and} \qquad f \circ g = \id_Y. \] If \(f\) has an inverse, \(f\) is invertible .

title: Definition 0.4.6 (Left and right inverses)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) . A function \(g \colon Y \to X\) is a left inverse of \(f\) if \(g \circ f = \id_X\) , and a right inverse of \(f\) if \(f \circ g = \id_Y\) .

content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(A_1, A_2 \subseteq X\) . Prove that \(f(A_1 \cup A_2) = f(A_1) \cup f(A_2)\) . Prove that \(f(A_1 \cap A_2) \subseteq f(A_1) \cap f(A_2)\) . Using \(q(x) = x^2\) on \(\nR\) , give an example where the inclusion in (b) is strict.

title: Exercise (C1: Left inverses are not unique)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be injective but not surjective, with \(X\) having at least two elements. Prove that \(f\) has at least two different left inverses. Find two different left inverses of \(f \colon \nN \to \nN\) , \(f(n) = n + 1\) . Explain why a bijective function has exactly one left inverse. Hint for (a): look at the proof of @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective and ask where it made a free choice.

title: Exercise (C3: When images and preimages undo each other)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) . Prove that \(f(f^{-1}(B)) = B\) for every \(B \subseteq Y\) if and only if \(f\) is surjective. Prove that \(f^{-1}(f(A)) = A\) for every \(A \subseteq X\) if and only if \(f\) is injective. Hint: for each direction you need only one well-chosen set; try a one-element set.

title: Proposition 0.4.1 (Image and preimage inclusions)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) , \(A \subseteq X\) and \(B \subseteq Y\) . Then \[ f\big(f^{-1}(B)\big) \subseteq B \qquad \text{and} \qquad A \subseteq f^{-1}\big(f(A)\big). \]

title: Theorem 0.4.7 (Bijective if and only if invertible)
content: A function \(f \colon X \to Y\) is invertible if and only if it is bijective. Moreover, an inverse of \(f\) , when it exists, is unique ; we denote it \(f^{-1} \colon Y \to X\) .

title: Theorem 0.4.2 (Associativity of composition)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) , \(g \colon Y \to Z\) and \(h \colon Z \to W\) be functions. Then \((h \circ g) \circ f = h \circ (g \circ f)\) .

title: Theorem 0.4.4 (Partial converse for compositions)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be functions. If \(g \circ f\) is injective, then \(f\) is injective. If \(g \circ f\) is surjective, then \(g\) is surjective.

title: Theorem 0.4.3 (Composition preserves injectivity and surjectivity)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be functions. If \(f\) and \(g\) are injective, then \(g \circ f\) is injective. If \(f\) and \(g\) are surjective, then \(g \circ f\) is surjective. If \(f\) and \(g\) are bijective, then \(g \circ f\) is bijective.

title: Theorem 0.4.9 (Injective iff surjective for finite sets of equal size)
content: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite sets with \(\lvert X \rvert = \lvert Y \rvert\) , and let \(f \colon X \to Y\) . Then \(f\) is injective if and only if \(f\) is surjective. In that case \(f\) is bijective.

title: Theorem 0.4.8 (Inverse of a composition)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be bijective. Then \(g \circ f\) is bijective and \[ (g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}. \]

title: Theorem 0.4.5 (Left inverses and injectivity)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) with \(X\) non-empty . Then \(f\) has a left inverse if and only if \(f\) is injective.

title: Theorem 0.4.6 (Right inverses and surjectivity)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) . Then \(f\) has a right inverse if and only if \(f\) is surjective.

title: Definition 0.5.3 (Equivalence class)
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on \(X\) , and let \(x \in X\) . The equivalence class of \(x\) is \[ [x] \coloneqq \{ y \in X : y \sim x \}. \] Any element of \([x]\) is called a representative of the class.

title: Definition 0.5.2 (Equivalence relation)
content: A relation \(\sim\) on a set \(X\) is an equivalence relation if it satisfies the following three conditions. Reflexive: \(x \sim x\) for every \(x \in X\) . Symmetric: for all \(x, y \in X\) , if \(x \sim y\) then \(y \sim x\) . Transitive: for all \(x, y, z \in X\) , if \(x \sim y\) and \(y \sim z\) then \(x \sim z\) .

title: Definition 0.5.4 (Partition)
content: A partition of a set \(X\) is a collection \(\mathcal{P}\) of subsets of \(X\) , called blocks , such that: every block is non-empty ; distinct blocks are disjoint: if \(B, B' \in \mathcal{P}\) and \(B \ne B'\) , then \(B \cap B' = \varnothing\) ; the blocks cover \(X\) : every \(x \in X\) lies in some block.

title: Definition 0.5.5 (Quotient set)
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on \(X\) . The quotient set of \(X\) by \(\sim\) is the set of all equivalence classes, \[ X/{\sim} \coloneqq \{ [x] : x \in X \}. \] The function \(\pi \colon X \to X/{\sim}\) , \(\pi(x) = [x]\) , is the quotient map .

title: Definition 0.5.1 (Relation)
content: A relation on a set \(X\) is a subset \(R \subseteq X \times X\) . When \((x, y) \in R\) we say \(x\) is related to \(y\) and write \(x \mathrel{R} y\) , or \(x \sim y\) when the relation is fixed.

title: Lemma 0.5.1 (Classes are equal or disjoint)
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on \(X\) , and let \(a, b \in X\) . \([a] = [b]\) if and only if \(a \sim b\) . Either \([a] = [b]\) or \([a] \cap [b] = \varnothing\) .

title: Theorem 0.5.2 (Equivalence relations and partitions)
content: Let \(X\) be a set. If \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation on \(X\) , then the set of its equivalence classes is a partition of \(X\) . If \(\mathcal{P}\) is a partition of \(X\) , then the relation “ \(x \sim_{\mathcal{P}} y\) if \(x\) and \(y\) lie in the same block” is an equivalence relation on \(X\) , and its equivalence classes are exactly the blocks of \(\mathcal{P}\) . The two constructions undo each other: starting from \(\sim\) , the relation defined in (b) by the partition in (a) is \(\sim\) again.

title: Theorem 0.5.3 (Functions on a quotient)
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on \(X\) , let \(\pi \colon X \to X/{\sim}\) be the quotient map, and let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. If \(f(a) = f(b)\) whenever \(a \sim b\) , then there is exactly one function \(\bar f \colon X/{\sim} \to Y\) with \(\bar f([x]) = f(x)\) for every \(x \in X\) , that is, \(\bar f \circ \pi = f\) . Conversely, if some function \(\bar f \colon X/{\sim} \to Y\) satisfies \(\bar f \circ \pi = f\) , then \(f(a) = f(b)\) whenever \(a \sim b\) .

title: Definition 0.6.1 (Complex Numbers)
content:
The set of complex numbers is \(
C \coloneqq 
R^2 = \{ (a, b) : a, b \in 
R \}\) , with addition and multiplication defined for every \((a, b), (c, d) \in 
C\) by \[ (a, b) + (c, d) \coloneqq (a + c, \; b + d), \qquad (a, b)(c, d) \coloneqq (ac - bd, \; ad + bc). \] We write \(a\) for \((a, 0)\) and \(i\) for \((0, 1)\) , so that \((a, b) = a + bi\) . For \(z = a + bi\) with \(a, b \in 
R\) , the real part of \(z\) is \(\operatorname{Re} z \coloneqq a\) and the imaginary part of \(z\) is \(\operatorname{Im} z \coloneqq b\) .

title: Definition 0.6.2 (Conjugate and Modulus)
content: Let \(z = a + bi \in \nC\) with \(a, b \in \nR\) . The complex conjugate of \(z\) is \(\conj{z} \coloneqq a - bi\) . The modulus (or absolute value) of \(z\) is the real number \(\lvert z \rvert \coloneqq \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \ge 0\) , the non-negative square root.

title: Proposition 0.6.1 (Arithmetic Laws in \nC)
content: For all \(z, w, u \in \nC\) : \(z + w = w + z\) and \(zw = wz\) ; \((z + w) + u = z + (w + u)\) and \((zw)u = z(wu)\) ; \(z(w + u) = zw + zu\) ; \(z + 0 = z\) , \(z \cdot 1 = z\) , and \(z + (-z) = 0\) , where \(-(a + bi) \coloneqq (-a) + (-b)i\) .

title: Proposition 0.6.3 (Inverse of a Complex Number)
content: Let \(z \in \nC\) with \(z \ne 0\) . Then \(w \coloneqq \dfrac{1}{\lvert z \rvert^2} \, \conj{z}\) satisfies \(zw = 1\) . We write \(z^{-1}\) or \(\dfrac{1}{z}\) for this \(w\) .

title: Theorem 0.6.4 (Triangle Inequality)
content: For all \(z, w \in \nC\) , \[ \lvert z + w \rvert \le \lvert z \rvert + \lvert w \rvert. \]

title: Theorem 0.6.2 (Properties of Conjugation and Modulus)
content: For all \(z, w \in \nC\) : \(\conj{z + w} = \conj{z} + \conj{w}\) and \(\conj{\conj{z}} = z\) ; \(\conj{zw} = \conj{z} \, \conj{w}\) ; \(z \conj{z} = \lvert z \rvert^2\) and \(z + \conj{z} = 2 \operatorname{Re} z\) ; \(\lvert zw \rvert = \lvert z \rvert \, \lvert w \rvert\) and \(\lvert \conj{z} \rvert = \lvert z \rvert\) .

title: Theorem 0.6.6 (De Moivre’s Formula)
content: For every \(\theta \in \nR\) and every \(n \in \nN\) , \[ \big(e^{i\theta}\big)^n = e^{in\theta}, \quad \text{that is,} \quad (\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i \sin n\theta. \] Consequently \((r e^{i\theta})^n = r^n e^{in\theta}\) for every real \(r > 0\) .

title: Theorem 0.6.7 (Fundamental Theorem of Algebra)
content:
Let \(n \ge 1\) and let \(a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in 
C\) with \(a_n 
e 0\) . Then there exists \(z \in 
C\) with \[ a_n z^n + a_{n-1} z^{n-1} + \dots + a_1 z + a_0 = 0. \]

title: Theorem 0.6.5 (Multiplication in Polar Form)
content: For all \(\theta, \varphi \in \nR\) , \[ e^{i\theta} e^{i\varphi} = e^{i(\theta + \varphi)}. \] Consequently, if \(z = r e^{i\theta}\) and \(w = s e^{i\varphi}\) with \(r, s > 0\) , then \(zw = rs \, e^{i(\theta + \varphi)}\) .

title: Definition 0.7.2 (Characteristic)
content: Let \(F\) be a field. If there is a positive integer \(n\) with \(n \cdot 1 = 0\) , the characteristic of \(F\) is the smallest such \(n\) . If there is no such \(n\) , the characteristic of \(F\) is \(0\) .

title: Definition 0.7.1 (Field)
content: A field is a set \(F\) together with two functions, addition \(+ \colon F \times F \to F\) , \((a, b) \mapsto a + b\) , and multiplication \(\cdot \colon F \times F \to F\) , \((a, b) \mapsto a \cdot b = ab\) , satisfying the following axioms. \(a + b = b + a\) for all \(a, b \in F\) . \((a + b) + c = a + (b + c)\) for all \(a, b, c \in F\) . There exists an element \(0 \in F\) such that \(a + 0 = a\) for every \(a \in F\) . For every \(a \in F\) there exists an element \(-a \in F\) such that \(a + (-a) = 0\) . \((ab)c = a(bc)\) for all \(a, b, c \in F\) . \(ab = ba\) for all \(a, b \in F\) . There exists an element \(1 \in F\) with \(1 \ne 0\) such that \(a \cdot 1 = a\) for every \(a \in F\) . For every non-zero \(a \in F\) there exists an element \(a^{-1} \in F\) such that \(a a^{-1} = 1\) . \(a(b + c) = ab + ac\) for all \(a, b, c \in F\) .

title: Exercise (B1: The Remaining Basic Properties)
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(a, b, c \in F\) . Using only the axioms and the parts of @thm-field-basic-properties proved in the text, prove: the element \(1\) in (F7) is unique; if \(ab = ac\) and \(a \ne 0\) , then \(b = c\) ; for \(a \ne 0\) , the inverse \(a^{-1}\) is unique; \((-1)a = -a\) . Hint: for (d), show that \(a + (-1)a = 0\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Solving Equations in \nF_7)
content: Solve \(3x + 5 = 2\) in \(\nF_7\) . Solve the system \(x + 2y = 3\) , \(3x + y = 1\) over \(\nF_7\) .

title: Exercise (C1: A Field with Four Elements)
content:
Let \(F = \{ a + b\alpha : a, b \in 
F_2 \}\) , a set of four formal symbols \(0, 1, \alpha,  eta\) , where \( eta \coloneqq 1 + \alpha\) . Define \[ (a + b\alpha) + (c + d\alpha) \coloneqq (a + c) + (b + d)\alpha, \qquad (a + b\alpha)(c + d\alpha) \coloneqq (ac + bd) + (ad + bc + bd)\alpha, \] with all coefficient arithmetic in \(
F_2\) . (The product is what expanding gives if we replace \(\alpha^2\) by \(\alpha + 1\) .) Write out the addition and multiplication tables of \(F\) . Prove that \(F\) is a field. Explain why there is no bijection \(\varphi \colon F 	o

title: Exercise (C2: Finite Fields Have Prime Characteristic)
content: Let \(F\) be a finite field. Prove that the characteristic of \(F\) is a prime \(p\) . Let \(F\) be a field of characteristic \(p > 0\) . Prove that \(p \cdot a = 0\) for every \(a \in F\) . Hint: for (a), the elements \(1 \cdot 1, 2 \cdot 1, 3 \cdot 1, \dots\) cannot all be different.

title: Exercise (C3: The Frobenius Identity)
content: Let \(p\) be a prime. Let \(a, b \in \nZ\) with \(p\) dividing \(ab\) . Prove that \(p\) divides \(a\) or \(p\) divides \(b\) . Deduce that \(p\) divides the binomial coefficient \(\binom{p}{k}\) for \(0 < k < p\) . Let \(F\) be a field of characteristic \(p\) . Prove that \((x + y)^p = x^p + y^p\) for all \(x, y \in F\) . You may use the binomial theorem \((x + y)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} \cdot (x^k y^{n-k})\) in any field, with integer multiples as in @lem-integer-multiples ; its inductive proof uses only the field axioms. Hint: for (a), use @lem-bezout-integers . For (b), use \(p! = \binom{p}{k}\, k!\, (p - k)!\) .

title: Lemma 0.7.2 (Bézout’s Lemma for Integers)
content: Let \(a, n \in \nZ\) with \(n \ge 1\) , and suppose that the only positive integer dividing both \(a\) and \(n\) is \(1\) . Then there exist \(x, y \in \nZ\) with \[ ax + ny = 1. \]

title: Lemma 0.7.4 (Integer Multiples)
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(a \in F\) and \(m, k \in \nN\) . Then \[ (m \cdot 1) + (k \cdot 1) = (m + k) \cdot 1, \qquad (m \cdot 1)(k \cdot 1) = (mk) \cdot 1, \qquad (m \cdot 1)\, a = m \cdot a. \]

title: Theorem 0.7.5 (The Characteristic Is 0 or Prime)
content: The characteristic of a field is either \(0\) or a prime number.

title: Theorem 0.7.1 (Basic Properties of Fields)
content: Let \(F\) be a field and let \(a, b, c \in F\) . The element \(0\) in (F3) is unique, and the element \(1\) in (F7) is unique. (Cancellation) If \(a + b = a + c\) , then \(b = c\) . If \(ab = ac\) and \(a \ne 0\) , then \(b = c\) . The negative \(-a\) in (F4) is unique, and for \(a \ne 0\) the inverse \(a^{-1}\) in (F8) is unique. \(0 \cdot a = 0\) . \((-1)a = -a\) . If \(ab = 0\) , then \(a = 0\) or \(b = 0\) .

title: Theorem 0.7.3 (\nZ/n\nZ Is a Field Exactly for Prime n)
content: Let \(n \ge 2\) be an integer. Then \(\nZ/n\nZ\) is a field if and only if \(n\) is prime.

title: Corollary 0.8.4 (No zero divisors in F[x])
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(p, q, r \in F[x]\) . If \(pq = 0\) , then \(p = 0\) or \(q = 0\) . If \(pq = pr\) and \(p \neq 0\) , then \(q = r\) .

title: Definition 0.8.3 (Degree)
content:
Let \(p = \sum a_k x^k \in F[x]\) . If \(p 
eq 0\) , the degree of \(p\) , written \(\deg p\) , is the largest \(n \in 
N\) with \(a_n 
eq 0\) . The coefficient \(a_n\) is the leading coefficient of \(p\) , and \(p\) is monic if its leading coefficient is \(1\) . The zero polynomial has degree \(\deg 0 = -\infty\) . We use the conventions \(-\infty < n\) and \(-\infty + n = n + (-\infty) = -\infty\) for every \(n \in 
N\) , and \(-\infty + (-\infty) = -\infty\) .

title: Definition 0.8.1 (Polynomial)
content:
Let \(F\) be a field. A polynomial over \(F\) in the indeterminate \(x\) is a sequence \((a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots)\) of elements of \(F\) , indexed by \(
N\) , such that only finitely many \(a_k\) are non-zero. That is, there is some \(N \in 
N\) with \(a_k = 0\) for every \(k > N\) . The element \(a_k\) is the coefficient of \(x^k\) . We write the polynomial as \[ p = a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + \dots + a_N x^N = \sum_{k=0}^{N} a_k x^k . \] Two polynomials \(p = \sum a_k x^k\) and \(q = \sum b_k x^k\) are equal if and only if \(a_k = b_k\) for every \(k \in 
N\) .

title: Definition 0.8.6 (Evaluation and roots)
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(p = \sum_{k=0}^{N} a_k x^k \in F[x]\) and \(c \in F\) . The value of \(p\) at \(c\) is the element \[ p(c) = \sum_{k=0}^{N} a_k c^k = a_0 + a_1 c + \dots + a_N c^N \in F , \] where \(c^0 = 1\) . An element \(c \in F\) is a root of \(p\) if \(p(c) = 0\) . The function \(F \to F\) , \(c \mapsto p(c)\) , is the polynomial function of \(p\) .

title: Definition 0.8.2 (The polynomial ring F[x])
content: Let \(F\) be a field. The set of all polynomials over \(F\) is denoted \(F[x]\) . For \(p = \sum a_k x^k\) and \(q = \sum b_k x^k\) in \(F[x]\) , define the sum \(p + q\) and the product \(pq\) by their coefficients: \[ p + q = \sum_{k} (a_k + b_k) x^k, \qquad pq = \sum_{k} \Bigl( \sum_{i=0}^{k} a_i b_{k-i} \Bigr) x^k . \]

title: Definition 0.8.4 (Polynomials of degree at most n)
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(n \in \nN\) . The set of polynomials over \(F\) of degree at most \(n\) is \[ F[x]_{\le n} = \{ p \in F[x] : \deg p \le n \} = \{ a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^n : a_0, \dots, a_n \in F \} . \]

title: Definition 0.8.5 (Polynomials of degree exactly n)
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(n \in \nN\) . The set of polynomials over \(F\) of degree exactly \(n\) is \[ F[x]_{= n} = \{ p \in F[x] : \deg p = n \} = \{ a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^n : a_0, \dots, a_n \in F, \ a_n \neq 0 \} . \]

title: Example (Comparing the two notations)
content: For each of \(x^2 + 1\) , \(3x - 2\) and \(0\) , decide whether it lies in \(\nR[x]_{\le 2}\) and whether it lies in \(\nR[x]_{= 2}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Degree of a composition)
content: For \(p = \sum_{k=0}^{m} a_k x^k\) and \(q\) in \(F[x]\) , define the composition \(p \circ q = \sum_{k=0}^{m} a_k q^k \in F[x]\) , where \(q^0 = 1\) . Prove that if \(p\) and \(q\) are non-constant, then \(\deg(p \circ q) = \deg p \cdot \deg q\) . Give an example showing the formula fails when \(q\) is constant. Hint: first find \(\deg(q^k)\) .
